newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: FEATURE - Dutch airport expansion sparks controversy.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Dutch airport expansion sparks controversy.

text.p: As Europe's fastest-growing civil aviation hub, Amsterdam's Schiphol Airport could become a victim of its own success unless government approves its daring -- and expensive -- plans to take to the water.
With a population of some 15.5 million squeezed into just over 41,000 square kilometres, the Netherlands has become famous for rolling back the sea in its quest for more space.
But Schiphol's plans for offshore expansion have run into fierce opposition from the country's environmental lobby, while users have also expressed reservations.

More than 80 interest groups, ranging from Dutch national carrier KLM to a Friends of the Earth affiliate, Milieudefensie, have voiced their opinions in a four-month public debate on the future of the Netherlands' air infrastructure.
"The plans presented by Schiphol will worsen rather than resolve the problems for nature and the environment," says Milieudefensie's Victor van den Belt.
"The idea is absurd -- the Netherlands is far too small to accommodate a mega-project in civil aviation like the expansion Schiphol is proposing," he adds.

At the other end of the scale, KLM favours the construction of a whole new airport: "Earmark a new location now for an airport for the 21st century," KLM president Pieter Bouw urged the government recently.
ENVIRONMENTAL NORMS LIMIT GROWTH

Government-imposed environmental norms have set a ceiling on Schiphol's growth of 44 million passengers and 3.3 million tonnes of freight a year, compared to a throughput of 28 million passengers and 1.3 million tonnes of goods in 1996.
But at current growth rates of around 12 percent per annum, the airport -- KLM's home base -- is set to reach its limits by 2003 or 2004.
Meanwhile environmentalists are urging more stringent regulations, calling for a standstill on carbon dioxide emissions at 1990 levels and a 75 percent reduction in serious noise nuisance.
"The existing environmental norms are butter-soft," said Van den Belt. "But Schiphol and others are already lobbying for the ceiling to be scrapped."
Backed by the transport sector and industry, Schiphol insists that further growth is essential to maintain the Netherlands' position as a key European distribution hub.
It argues that further expansion need not pose an extra burden on the environment, although the costs of a green solution will be considerable.

"There are various possibilities for accommodating further growth of air traffic in the Netherlands once Schiphol reaches the existing environmental limits on growth," airport president Hans Smits argues.
ISLAND SOLUTION GREEN BUT COSTLY
Schiphol's preferred option is the construction of a remote hub on an artificial island in the North Sea some 10 kilometres off the Dutch coast.
This would allow the necessary expansion while limiting the environmental burden, it argues.

However a major drawback is the cost, seen running to some 30 billion guilders ($15 billion), including the construction of a largely underground high-speed rail network to connect the remote runways with the main air terminal.

Two less costly ideas put forward by Schiphol are land reclamation in the Markermeer freshwater lake (22 to 28 billion guilders) or an overflow facility for charters and cargo on the Maasvlakte polder extension to the Rotterdam port complex (14 billion guilders).
So far the response from users has been lukewarm, with Schiphol's biggest customer KLM voicing misgivings about a dual location in any shape or form.
"The further expansion of Dutch (civil) aviation should continue to be concentrated at a single location," it said in a statement outlining its standpoint on the airport's future.
"The hub function of a home airport is of truly essential importance," KLM's Bouw elaborated in an interview in the latest issue of its in-house magazine.

"All routes intersect there...if you spread the handling process over two locations and your passengers have to sit in the train for 15 or 20 minutes before they can transfer to other flights, you lose your customers to carriers with better facilities," he said.
PASSENGERS TRANSFERS NEED SINGLE TERMINAL
KLM generates some 40 percent of all traffic through Schiphol airport, with transfer passengers accounting for around 60 percent of its clientele.
Until now the success of KLM's transfer product -- essential to revenue growth in view of its limited national market -- has leaned heavily on Schiphol's single terminal concept.
The airline has capitalised on the concentration of traffic at a single point, developing a so-called "wave" system to dovetail incoming and outgoing flights so as to cut transfer times to a minimum.
It is due to boost the number of "waves" from three to six some time next year.
Even with a 15-minute ceiling on travel times under the North Sea option, remote runways could eliminate KLM's current competitive edge, the airline fears.
Instead KLM would like to see the construction of a completely new one-terminal airport at a location to be earmarked by the government as soon as possible.
CARGO FORWARDERS LIKE MARKERMEER OPTION
Meanwhile air cargo forwarders are plumping for the Markermeer option, arguing that remote runways in the North Sea would preclude site development near the airport.
Markermeer would be a cheaper option as the polder would offer enough cheap space for distribution companies, Dutch Air Transport Association ATAN said in its report late last month.
A detailed report on the outcome of a July 2 conference to wrap up the debate has been passed to ministry officials, who will formulate recommendations to be presented to cabinet after the summer.
However the issue of airport expansion is unlikely to be finally decided this year, a traffic ministry spokesman said.
"With general elections due next May it remains to be seen whether the current administration will determine a stance on the issue," he said. ($ = 1.981 Dutch Guilders)
